title: The Stock Market Sounds an Alarm for the First Time in Nearly 27 Years. Here Is What History Says the S&P 500 Will Do Next.
detail:
The Stock Market Sounds an Alarm for the First Time in Nearly 27 Years. Here Is What History Says the S&P 500 Will Do Next.
Adam Spatacco, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 12:20 PM MST 5 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has gained 12% so far in 2026, extending a bull market fueled mostly by enthusiasm around artificial intelligence (AI). However, the rally has not been without some turbulence. Both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) recently witnessed sharp declines as investors grapple with sticky inflation, elevated bond yields, and concerns about how the AI revolution is being financed.

There's another reason investors should be cautious. The CAPE ratio and Buffett indicator suggest the stock market is historically expensive. In fact, the CAPE ratio has climbed above 40, a level previously sustained only during the dot-com bubble.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Does this mean the stock market is about to crash? Read on to find out.

The CAPE ratio has approached dot-com territory

The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio was popularized by economist Robert Shiller. A conventional price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio compares stock prices with earnings over a single year. By contrast, the CAPE ratio divides the S&P 500's price by the average of 10 years of inflation-adjusted earnings. By taking a longer-term view, CAPE readings smooth out fluctuations in profits affected by recessions or unusual booms.

Currently, the CAPE ratio hovers around 41, more than double its historical average of 17.8. Over 155 years worth of stock market data, the only other sustained period when the CAPE ratio exceeded 40 was during the dot-com bubble. It peaked around 44 in December 1999, shortly before technology stocks imploded.

Shiller CAPE Ratio data by YCharts

The Buffett indicator is flashing red

Another popular valuation metric is the Buffett indicator, aptly named after legendary investor Warren Buffett. The calculation is straightforward: Divide the total market capitalization of U.S. stocks by the country's annual gross domestic product (GDP). Currently, the Buffett indicator sits around 237%. This means the stock market is valued at $2.37 for every $1 of annual U.S. economic output.

While that might suggest stocks are egregiously overvalued, there are important reasons today's market differs from the dot-com era. For starters, many of today's largest companies are incredibly profitable. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia generate substantial revenue and cash flow. By contrast, many speculative internet companies that commanded astronomical valuations in the late 1990s never even generated sales, let alone turned a profit.

One business stands out at Home Depot (HD): SRS, an acquisition that now sells through Home Depot's stores and that bulls may be betting on. You probably see Home Depot as a store chain tied to housing. Management says housing turnover has been low for four years, and Home Depot stock lost 16.9% over the past year, while the S&P 500 gained 16.5%. That is the contradiction: a business that may be growing faster than the rest of Home Depot sits inside a stock that has trailed the market. So is SRS really growing faster than the rest of Home Depot?

SRS Is Outgrowing The Rest Of Home Depot

So far, yes. During the quarter that ended August 2, 2026, SRS grew its comparable sales faster than Home Depot as a whole. Overall comparable sales for the company rose 1.7%. SRS was positive in all of its verticals, and management said on the August 18, 2026 call that it looks to be taking significant share.

Management expects SRS to keep growing for the year. It guided the business to mid-single-digit organic sales growth for fiscal 2026. For the whole company, management guided a different measure, comparable sales growth of flat to 2%.

One number shows how far SRS has spread: 90%. That is the share of Home Depot's stores that closed a sale through SRS within the last 12 months, management said, so SRS no longer sits apart from the stores.

Home Depot's Margin Has Slipped For Three Years

Home Depot's profit has not kept up with SRS's growth so far. Its operating margin was 14.9% over the twelve months that ended July 30, 2023. The figure slipped to 13.9% a year later. Operating margin fell again to 13.1% in the twelve months to August 3, 2025 and to 12.4% in the twelve months to August 2, 2026. That marks the lowest rate at any of the past 40 quarter ends.

The latest quarter's gross margin looked better, and that is where the worry sits. On the same call, the question came up whether Home Depot would have missed profit forecasts without a tariff refund. Management said the company would have beaten its own expectations regardless. By management's count, the refund added about 145 basis points to gross margin, yet gross margin rose only about 25 basis points from a year earlier. About 60 basis points of it went to higher fuel, energy and input costs, and about 60 more went to the mix of the GMS and Mingledorff's acquisitions.

Home Depot does get more sales from those acquisitions. Management expects total sales to grow about 2.5% to 4.5% in fiscal 2026, reflecting the GMS acquisition, new stores, new branches and tuck-in acquisitions. But management also expects the unplanned input costs to fully offset the tariff refunds over the year.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.13% on October 21. That is already above the ceiling Alan Rechtschaffen expects for long-term rates. On the same day, UBS weighed in. UBS's senior portfolio manager laid out a case for the S&P 500 to reach 9,500 by June 2027.

Shutterstock

His target sits well above the UBS base case of 8,400 and above his own call for 8,100 by the end of 2026. He ties it to three long-running technology waves: superintelligence, longevity and disease cures, and energy.

Profits are his strongest evidence. He cited 25% year-over-year earnings growth. He expects double-digit gains next year, so the rally rests on what companies actually earn.

His rate path complicates the outlook. He expects the Fed to pause in October, probably raise rates in December and again in March, and only then consider cuts. A bull case that runs through two more hikes requires you to trust that productivity gains will outrun tighter money.

Profits Are Carrying This Rally

Earnings-driven gains hold up better than price-to-earnings expansion, because multiples can shrink quickly when rates move. For NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), fiscal second-quarter revenue grew 105.8% to $96.22 billion, with Data Center sales of $89.02 billion.

At Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Azure grew 43% and passed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time. Google Cloud revenue at Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) jumped 82%.

Double-digit growth next year depends on that spending continuing to turn into revenue. NVIDIA expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal year '28. That points to strong demand, but it also caps how fast the company can ship.

NXP Semiconductors recently saw its stock outperform the S&P 500 and investors are now focused on the upcoming October 27, 2026 earnings release, with expectations for higher year on year earnings and revenue.

The combination of anticipated earnings growth, a favorable analyst ranking and a P/E multiple below the broader industry is drawing attention to how NXP Semiconductors converts demand in automotive, industrial and IoT into sustained profit quality.

We will examine how NXP Semiconductors' investment narrative is shaped by rising earnings expectations ahead of the October 27 results announcement.

Scan how NXP Semiconductors lines up against other potential breakout chip and AI infrastructure plays by reviewing the 55 AI infrastructure stocks in one pass.

NXP Semiconductors Investment Narrative Recap

NXP Semiconductors is positioned as a company where auto, industrial and IoT demand could translate into steadier orders and support its margin structure. To stay comfortable as a shareholder, you need to believe the firm can turn its SDV and physical AI pipeline into ongoing design wins while managing its China autos and data center exposure gaps. The latest share price move and earnings buzz do not change that core thesis.

The near-term focus is the October 27 earnings report, because it will either reassure investors on guidance after the July pullback or keep questions alive around the wide forecast ranges. The biggest current risk sits in auto and China inventory, and any sign of correction there could matter more than a single quarter of headline growth.

The most relevant fresh data point is the expectation that NXP Semiconductors will report higher EPS and revenue than the prior-year quarter on October 27. That update sits directly within the investor debate about whether the auto and industrial pipelines can sustain the recent earnings growth rate of 38.4% reported over the past year.

If the release shows solid profitability and progress in automotive, industrial and IoT while the forward P/E remains below broader semiconductor averages, it may support the view that the business mix is shifting toward higher value segments. Any signs of pressure tied to Chinese auto demand or uncertainty around edge AI and data center control plane ambitions would keep execution risk in focus even if headline numbers appear healthy.

NXP Semiconductors' current analyst narrative points to revenues of US$17.6b and earnings of US$4.7b by 2029, based on a forecast revenue growth rate of 10.2% per year. That outlook assumes earnings today of US$3.0b, which implies an increase of about US$1.7b in consensus earnings by the 2029 forecast year.

title: Cathie Wood sells $16 million of surging tech stock

Cathie Wood sells $16 million of surging tech stock

Trading disclosure

Cathie Wood, head of Ark Investment Management, often takes profits when her favorite tech stocks rally.

That's what she's been doing with Palantir Technologies (PLTR), selling shares as the stock rallies ahead of its third-quarter earnings report.

Last year, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 11.05% as of Oct. 21, while the S&P 500 surged 13.32%, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 21, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -6.36%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 11.26% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood buys $11.8 million of tumbling tech stock

"I welcome the question. Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in a post on X on Oct. 5.

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries including healthcare, financial services and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

In September, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X, saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were orchestrated.

(Updates with latest market prices and developments.)

US benchmark equity indexes declined as renewed unease over artificial intelligence spending weighed on the technology sector.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 2.4% to 26,050.8 after midday Thursday, while the S&P 500 fell 1.3% to 7,658.5. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged down 0.1% to 52,791.5. Wall Street finished Wednesday trading higher, with the S&P 500 extending its winning streak to a third straight session.

Among sectors, tech led the laggards with a 2.8% decline intraday Thursday, while consumer staples paced the gainers.

Meta Platforms (META) shares tumbled 7.3% intraday. The Facebook parent expects capital expenditures in a range of $135 billion to $145 billion, reflecting a higher bottom end versus the previous guidance of $130 billion.

Meta vowed to continue investing aggressively to support its core business and AI initiatives.

Its quarterly free cash flow turned negative, Saxo Bank said in a report Thursday.

"The investor lesson: a profitable core business can finance ambitious projects, but growing revenue does not automatically translate into growing cash for shareholders," Saxo Bank said. "Meta faces the risk that AI infrastructure costs grow faster than the profits they generate."

Tesla's (TSLA) stock fell 2.1% intraday.

Tesla's disappointing third-quarter operating margin reflects a ramp in AI investments that could weigh on the electric vehicle manufacturer's near-term earnings, Truist Securities said in note on Wednesday.

Procter & Gamble (PG) was up 5.8%, the biggest gain on the Dow. The consumer goods giant lifted its full-year sales growth outlook to reflect an acquisition, while its fiscal first-quarter earnings unexpectedly increased year over year.

Moderna's (MRNA) shares plunged nearly 24% intraday, the biggest decline on the S&P 500, following a potential leak of data related to its personalized melanoma vaccine developed with Merck (MRK), Bloomberg reported. Merck was down 1.5%.

Treasury yields slumped intraday, with the two-year rate retreating by 17.3 basis points to 4.65% and the 10-year rate off 18.1 basis points to 4.97%.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil was up 2.2% at $99.30 a barrel intraday, while Brent climbed 3.3% to $112.44.

The US and Israel have drawn up specific plans to resume military operations against Iran after the midterm elections in November, The New York Times reported Wednesday, citing sources. The targets are likely to include Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone assets, according to the report.

The US has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid its ongoing conflict with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, CNBC reported.

Spot gold slid 2.3% to $4,047.57 per troy ounce, while silver lost 4.8% to $54.97 per ounce.

What Does The Market Want From Lowe's Stock?

Lowe's (LOW) stock lost 17.2% over the past year, while the S&P 500 returned 16.5%. You probably think of Lowe's as a store for do-it-yourself homeowners, and management says those shoppers are holding back. But management also says two acquisitions position Lowe's to win more business from larger professional contractors, its Pro customers. Buyers at today's price may be betting on that. So is Lowe's Pro business still growing while homeowners hold back?

Lowe's Pro Business Is Still Growing

Yes, so far: Management said Pro delivered another quarter of growth in the quarter ended July 31, 2026. Lowe's posted $26 billion in total sales for the quarter, up 8.3% from a year earlier.

Pro did not grow alone. Management said Online and Home Services, which serves customers who want the job done for them, joined Pro in helping offset softer do-it-yourself spending. Online sales grew 15.7%.

Lowe's has also put money behind Pro. Management says FBM and ADG, two acquired businesses that sell into residential construction, position the company to grow its share with larger Pro customers over the long term.

Is Lowe's Earning More As Its Sales Grow?

Not yet. Lowe's earned $2.4 billion in the quarter ended July 31, 2026. That matched its earnings from a year earlier on $2.0 billion more in sales.

Its operating margin slipped to 13.7% from 14.5% a year earlier. Management said gross margin was 80 basis points below the prior year's adjusted figure. That drop included the dilutive impact of the FBM and ADG acquisitions, which suggests the businesses Lowe's bought to reach Pro customers earn thinner margins than the rest of the company.

Where Could Lowe's Pro Push Fall Short?

Lowe's existing business is barely growing, and the businesses it bought sell into a weak market for new homes. Comparable sales rose just 0.2% in the quarter ended July 31, 2026, far below the rise in total sales. Comparable transactions fell 2.1%. Management attributed that decline to pressure in weather-sensitive outdoor and seasonal categories.

Management also expects continued pressure on FBM and ADG from new home construction, a market it describes as softer for longer. If Pro growth stalls, Lowe's is left depending on do-it-yourself demand. Management calls that demand an important driver of its overall performance and says it remains under pressure.

If profit does not follow the sales, those extra sales do little for shareholders. For now, management expects adjusted earnings per share in the third quarter to be about 7% below a year earlier.
